Congratulations: we are very pleased to inform you that your article, "Primate TRIM5 proteins form hexagonal nets on HIV-1 capsids", has been accepted for publication in eLife. The Reviewing Editor for your submission was Stephen Goff and the Senior Editor was Wenhui Li.

All three of our reviewers were enthused about the findings and the paper. They all summarized the salient points and raised only very minor points that can be readily addressed.

Reviewer #1 (General assessment and major comments (Required)):

The authors previously reported that TRIM5 forms a planar, hexagonal lattice and generated a model for how the TRIM5 subdomains are arranged. These experiments were limited in terms of detail and the use of a TRIM5 fusion protein (TRIM5-21R). Here electron cryotomograms (ECT) with full-length and SPRY-deleted TRIM5-21R confirmed the placement of the SPRY domain at the middle of the hexagon edges. The authors then developed a method for generating full-length, authentic TRIM5 proteins and confirmed hexameric lattice formation with 2 TRIM5 orthologues. 2D CA crystals were assembled and dimeric TRIM5 was added under conditions that preclude spontaneous lattice formation by TRIM5. CA-templated assembly was observed with 3 restricting TRIM5s but not with 2 non-restrictive TRIM5s. The purified TRIM5s co-sedimented with recombinant, crosslinked CA tubes. Negative stain and deep-etch EM demonstrated thin nets on the surface of the CA tubes when restrictive TRIM5s were added, but not with controls. The authors made virion cores by detergent extraction and density sedimentation gradient, expertly increasing the core yield with CA A14C/E45C/A92E, and enrichment on cyclophilin A columns. Cores were then incubated with TRIM5 protein and visualized by ECT. Hexagonal nets of TRIM5 were visualized and modeled. This expert body of work shows how restriction factor TRIM5 associates with HIV-1 cores. I have a few minor comments that might help the reader.

Reviewer #1 (Minor Comments):

1) Figure 1C and D: The density difference map in 1E does not seem to match the difference of the representative images shown in the bottom middle panels of 1C and D. It looks like TRIM5-21R-ΔSPRY retains density in the middle of the hexagon edges. Perhaps the authors could clarify this?

2) Concerning TRIM5 purification (subsection “Expression and purification of authentic primate TRIM5α and TRIMCyp proteins”) the authors should acknowledge that another group reported detailed methods for baculo expression and purification of high concentration, authentic TRIM5 from owl monkey (Pertel et al., 2011). Regarding the discussion at the end of the subsection “Reagent development”, this same group also used A14C/E45C stabilized CA cores to stimulate the Ubx E3 activity of purified TRIM5 protein.

3) Figure 3 shows the templated assembly of restrictive TRIM5 on 2D CA lattices. Images with a non-restrictive TRIM5 might help the reader visualize the differences.

4) Figure 4C: The authors state that co-assembly of CA with TRIM5 was more efficient than if TRIM5 was added after CA was preformed into tubes (at the end of the subsection “TRIM5 binding to helical HIV-1 CA tubes”). This statement seems at odds with the histogram in Figure 4C which shows pretty much the same percentages of "Rings on preformed CA tubes" with "Rings on co-assembly".

5) In the subsection “Generation of hyperstable, disulfide-crosslinked HIV-1 core particle”: I don't understand the calculations stated in the text regarding Figure 5A: “[…] a substantial fraction of the CA protein also concentrated at the density expected for native core particles (fractions 10-12, highlighted in pink in Figure 5A, right panel). These "hyperstable" cores were reproducibly recovered in higher yields (0.8 ± 1%) than wild type cores (0.2 ± 0.1%)[…] “Fraction 10 looks to be 25%, not 0.8%?

Reviewer #2 (General assessment and major comments (Required)):

In their manuscript, Li and coworkers report the purification of milligram quantities of TRIM5 restriction factor proteins and structural analysis of complexes of some of them with purified HIV-1 cores and assemblies of recombinant HIV-1 CA protein. The authors also describe a new approach they developed to purify HIV-1 cores from virions. The study represents a significant advance because: (1) TRIM5 proteins have been notoriously difficult to purify, and (2) interactions of TRIM5α with native HIV-1 cores have not been described in the literature. Based on their structural results, the authors conclude that TRIM5 proteins form hexagonal "nets" around the viral capsid resembling those formed spontaneously by the restriction factors. Assuming the technique employed for purifying TRIM5 proteins is robust, this study should greatly facilitate future studies of TRIM5 structure and biochemistry.

I have no significant criticisms.

Reviewer #2 (Minor Comments):

Introduction, third paragraph: the term "viral core replication particle." I don't recall reading this term previously, and it seems like an odd combination of adjectives and nouns.

At the end of the subsection “Structure-based models for TRIM5-21R assembly”: “[…]thereby validating the model[…] “According to Merriam-Webster, the word "validate” implies establishing validity by authoritative affirmation or by factual proof. I suggest replacing this with "supporting."

Reviewer #3 (General assessment and major comments (Required)):

Li et al. report on a fairly comprehensive structural study focused on the nature of the interaction between TRIM5α and incoming retroviral capsid cores. The results to some extent confirm expectations based on highly artificial systems, and greatly extend these through extensive efforts to use bona fide, purified TRIM5α proteins together with capsid preps as close as possible to native structures. This is an important step forward – despite intense focus on TRIM5 and TRIM5-mediated restriction, standard approaches to understanding protein interactions have not been useful. As the authors point out, the methods may also be applicable to the study of the many other known capsid-interacting co-factors in the cell. Another strength of the study is that most results apply to two or more distinct TRIM5 homologs, confirming the generality of the findings. The model is also consistent with known interactions and with the observation that TRIM5-mediated restriction is saturable.

The results also begin to fill in/suggest aspects of mechanism that will certainly drive further work by both structural and cellular laboratories, and this will be a great strength of the paper. Interesting details emerging from the study include the likely intermolecular dimerization of RING domains upon assembly, which suggests a regulatory mechanism that among other things may control the E3 Ub ligase activity in the absence of a target or before sufficient assembly has occurred on the target, and the orientation of the RING domains on the exposed surface of the lattice. Results also indicate that the formation of a hexagonal lattice is a conserved mechanism, and open the door for structural studies to understand both the broad spectrum of retroviruses that can be recognized while also trying to understand how, at the same time, individual retroviruses can "escape" this interaction while maintaining integral capsid functions. It potentially may suggest how other TRIM proteins recognize their respective ligands.

Overall this is an important study and it should have a significant impact on the field.

results.result: Electron cryotomography (ECT) of TRIM5-21R and TRIM5-21RΔSPRY revealed that both proteins assemble into similar planar hexagonal lattices, and difference density maps localized the SPRY domains to the center of each hexagon edge.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are well-supported by the ECT data presented in Figure 1C-E. The experimental approach is clearly described, the structural observations are consistent with prior 2D projection data, and the difference density analysis provides direct evidence for SPRY domain localization.

results.result: TRIM5-21R lattices exhibit considerable conformational variability, with hexamer edge lengths varying by up to ±5 nm (centered at 19 nm) and vertex angles varying by up to ±20° (centered at 120°), explaining the poor crystalline order and modest diffraction resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 are supported by quantitative measurements from ECT data shown in Figure 1F-G. The nearest neighbor analysis provides objective evidence for lattice variability, and the inference that this variability explains poor diffraction is logical and well-reasoned.

results.result: A baculoviral expression system in insect cells was developed to purify authentic primate TRIM5 proteins to >95% purity with yields of 1.3-9.6 mg/L. Proteins remained dimeric and soluble under low salt, alkaline conditions, and a proteolysis-resistant TRIMCyp mutant (K283D,Q287D) retained HIV-1 restriction activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C68 describe a comprehensive protein purification protocol supported by SDS-PAGE (Figure 2A-B), gel filtration data (C64), mass spectrometry (C66), and functional assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The methods are well-documented and the results are reproducible.

results.result: TRIM5αAGMpyg and TRIMCyp spontaneously assembled into 2D hexagonal arrays similar to TRIM5-21R, demonstrating that diverse primate TRIM5 proteins sharing 73% pairwise identity across TRIM domains can form analogous hexagonal nets, though assembly efficiencies varied.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C76 are supported by EM images (Figure 2C-D) and 2D projection reconstructions showing similar hexagonal ring structures across different TRIM5 proteins. The conclusion about conservation is well-justified by the structural similarity despite sequence divergence.

results.result: Three restricting TRIM5 proteins assembled into visible hexagonal nets on preformed HIV-1 CA crystal surfaces, while non-restricting proteins did not, demonstrating that templated assembly correlates with restriction activity and emphasizing the coupling of CA binding and TRIM5 lattice assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 are supported by EM images (Figure 3) and Fourier transform analysis showing hexagonal TRIM5 lattices on CA crystals only for restricting variants. The correlation between templated assembly and restriction activity is clear and well-documented.

results.result: TRIM5αAGMpyg and TRIMCypK283D,Q287D bound specifically to disulfide-crosslinked helical CA tubes as demonstrated by co-sedimentation assays, and four restricting TRIM5 proteins formed ring-like decorations on CA tube surfaces that correlated with restriction activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C90 are supported by co-sedimentation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) with appropriate controls (ΔSPRY and cyclosporine A) and EM images (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) showing decorations only for restricting TRIM5 proteins.

results.result: TRIM5 proteins formed hexagonal nets on helical HIV-1 CA tubes, with more extensive lattices observed during co-assembly of TRIM5 and CA proteins. ECT revealed networks of hexagonal nets with edge lengths predominantly ~19 nm (varying 15-23 nm) and vertex angles averaging ~120° (ranging 80-160°).
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C104 are supported by deep-etch EM (Figure 4A), negative stain EM (Figure 4B), ECT (Figure 4D, Video 1), and quantitative measurements (Figure 4C, 4E). The observation that co-assembly produces more extensive lattices is well-documented.

results.result: Disulfide crosslinks at CA positions A14C and E45C spontaneously formed in HIV-1 capsids, stabilizing cores without major morphological defects. Hyperstable CAA14C,E45C cores were recovered in 4-fold higher yields (0.8±1%) than wild type cores (0.2±0.1%), with nearly all CA molecules crosslinked within stable hexamers.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C119 are supported by sucrose gradient purification data (Figure 5A), EM morphology analysis (Figure 5B), and non-reducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 5C). The quantitative yield improvements and crosslinking efficiency are well-documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: An affinity purification method using OSF-CypA increased hyperstable core yields 4-fold (3±2%) and improved purity. The CA A92E mutation reduced core clustering without affecting TRIM5α restriction, morphology, or yields (3±1%). Purified cores contained expected viral proteins and were fully crosslinked.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C131 are supported by the affinity purification scheme (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E), quantitative yield data, EM images (Figure 5D-E), SDS-PAGE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), and citations to prior work showing A92E does not affect restriction.

results.result: Restricting TRIM5 proteins (TRIM5αAGMpyg and TRIM5αrh) bound directly to hyperstable HIV-1 cores at near-saturating levels (measured TRIM5:CA ratio 1:7±2, estimated saturation 1:14), while non-restricting TRIM5αcpz did not bind. EM revealed ring-like TRIM5αrh assemblies on core surfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C140 are supported by co-sedimentation assays (Figure 6A) with quantitative stoichiometry measurements, restriction assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and EM images (Figure 6B). The correlation between binding and restriction is clear.

results.result: ECT of TRIM5α-decorated HIV-1 cores revealed that ~12% of cores were decorated with TRIM5α hexagonal nets showing ~19 nm arms. Crosslinking with Sulfo-EGS increased decoration prevalence, revealing extensive but irregular TRIM5α hexagonal nets (edge lengths 20±2 nm, vertex angles 120±2°) that sometimes enveloped entire capsids.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C152 are supported by ECT data (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1-3, Videos 2-4) with quantitative measurements. The observation that crosslinking increases decoration prevalence is well-documented, though the loss of TRIM5α to the air/water interface represents a technical limitation.

results.result: Rigid body fitting of B-box 2 trimer and coiled-coil dimer crystal structures into ECT density maps revealed that each hexagon edge is occupied by a TRIM5α coiled-coil dimer and three-fold vertices by three B-box 2 domains, with good agreement in dimensions and angles. TRIM5 proteins form flexible hexagonal nets on capsid surfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C158 are supported by the structural fitting shown in Figure 7C and the schematic model in Figure 7D. The fitting demonstrates consistency between crystal structures and ECT densities, though the authors appropriately note this is coarse fitting without geometric optimization.

results.result: Structural modeling indicates that each hexagon edge (~19 nm) accommodates the antiparallel TRIM5α coiled-coil (~17 nm), with RING and B-box 2 domains associating at three-fold vertices. The L2 linkers fold back to form a four-helix bundle at the coiled-coil center.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by measurements from EM data, structural modeling, and consistency with the trimeric B-box 2 structure from the accompanying paper (Wagner et al., 2016). The dimensional compatibility between hexagon edges and coiled-coil length is well-established.

results.result: The studies support models that TRIM5 restriction factors bind directly to retroviral capsid surfaces with restriction susceptibility dictated by capsid recognition. Hexagonal net assembly is conserved across primate TRIM5 proteins, with each ring edge formed by a TRIM5 dimer displaying two SPRY/CypA domains. Capsid binding and TRIM5 assembly are coupled processes promoting high-affinity, specific recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C163 represent well-supported conclusions synthesizing multiple lines of evidence from binding assays, assembly studies, structural analyses, and functional data. The conclusions are appropriately supported by citations to prior work and the current study's findings.

results.result: TRIM5 proteins overcome retroviral capsid variability by coupling weak recognition of conserved epitopes with hexagonal net assembly, amplifying binding through avidity. Hexagonal net assembly is conserved but not highly regular, with this flexibility potentially required to adapt to irregular retroviral capsids.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C171 synthesize the pattern recognition model with the observed structural variability. The interpretation that flexibility enables recognition of irregular capsids is logical and supported by the data, though the mechanistic link remains somewhat speculative (appropriately qualified with 'may be required').

results.result: The L2 linker platform could buttress and orient the TRIM5α SPRY domains.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is speculative ('could, in principle') and lacks direct experimental evidence. While the structural model places the L2 linker platform near the SPRY domains, the functional role in orienting SPRY domains has not been tested.

results.result: The flexibility of TRIM5 assembly may reflect flexing of coiled-coil domains and/or hinges, and the two lattices (TRIM5 and CA) could template one another during co-assembly to optimize interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C102 and C105 are speculative interpretations ('may reflect', 'presumably because') without direct experimental evidence. While the interpretations are reasonable, they represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms.

results.result: Non-native CAA14C,E45C assemblies probably arose from spurious crosslinking of CA hexamers in the free intraviral pool excluded from mature capsids.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is a reasonable interpretation supported by citations about free CA pools, but the origin of the non-native assemblies has not been directly demonstrated. Alternative explanations (e.g., crosslinking during purification) are not excluded.

results.result: TRIM5α was being lost to the air/water interface during plunge-freezing.
results.evaluation: Claim C148 is an interpretation of the observation that TRIM5α was prevalent at the air/water interface with few decorated cores. While plausible, the mechanism and timing of TRIM5α loss have not been directly demonstrated. The crosslinking experiments (C149-C150) support but do not prove this interpretation.

results.result: Longer TRIM5α densities (~38 nm) might occur through association of two TRIM5α dimer sets via dimeric rather than trimeric B-box 2 interactions.
results.evaluation: Claim C154 is speculative ('might occur') with limited supporting evidence. The observation of ~38 nm densities is noted but not shown ('data not shown'), and the proposed mechanism is hypothetical, though supported by citation to the accompanying paper.

results.result: Hyperstable capsids may represent a useful starting point for developing in vitro viral replication assays.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 is purely speculative about future applications without any supporting data. The conditional statement ('particularly if disulfides can be reduced without inactivating enzymes') highlights that this remains untested.

results.result: Two RING domains at three-fold vertices may form an active dimer with the third 'orphan' RING domain used for autoubiquitylation. Formation of hexagonal TRIM5 lattices may activate the ubiquitin signaling cascade leading to capsid dissociation and reverse transcription inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C190 and C193 are speculative mechanistic proposals ('suggests', 'may') based on structural observations and prior work on RING domain function and autoubiquitylation. While the model is plausible and supported by structural data (C189, C191, C192), direct experimental evidence for this specific mechanism is lacking.

results.result: Background claims establishing prior knowledge about TRIM5 proteins, retroviral capsids, and the pattern recognition model.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C38 represent established knowledge and prior work appropriately supported by citations. These provide necessary context for the current study and accurately represent the state of the field.

results.result: Methods were developed for preparing authentic recombinant TRIM5 proteins, TRIM5-CA co-assemblies, and stable HIV-1 cores, which were used to demonstrate that TRIM5 proteins form hexagonal arrays on HIV-1 capsids.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 accurately summarize the methodological advances and key findings of the study. These are well-supported by the detailed experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: TRIM5 proteins assembled into hexagonal nets comprising open hexameric rings with SPRY domains on edges and B-box/RING domains at vertices. The principles of hexagonal assembly and capsid pattern recognition are conserved across primates, allowing conformational plasticity to recognize diverse retroviral capsids.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 represent the core findings of the abstract, well-supported by the comprehensive structural and biochemical data presented throughout the manuscript. The conclusion about conservation and plasticity is justified by the observation of similar structures across multiple TRIM5 proteins with variable lattice parameters.

results.result: Prior work on TRIM5α purification has been limited to impure proteins, fragments, or non-native constructs because TRIM5α proteins tend to self-assemble.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 accurately describe limitations of prior work, supported by citations. This establishes the significance of the current study's purification methods.

results.result: Helical CA tubes provide a regularized model for curved, symmetric CA hexagon arrays on conical capsid surfaces.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by citations to prior work establishing CA tubes as a model system. This justifies their use in the current study.

results.result: Retrovirus susceptibility to TRIM5 restriction varies dramatically and is determined largely at the capsid recognition level.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 represents established knowledge supported by multiple citations. This provides important context for the study's focus on capsid binding.

results.result: Recombinant TRIM5αrh proteins have been used to generate monoclonal antibodies. Different TRIM5 domains work together as an integrated machine, making it important to study intact proteins to understand capsid recognition coupled to ubiquitin signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C167 describe applications of the purified proteins and justify the importance of studying intact TRIM5 proteins, supported by citations. These highlight the significance of the methodological advances.

results.result: Multiple TRIM5 molecules can bind continuously to capsids in cells (stoichiometry unknown), and in vitro TRIM5 can cover most of the capsid surface. A patch of 4-6 TRIM5 rings (~40 recognition domains) covers about half the capsid surface, suggesting complete envelopment is not required for restriction, consistent with CA mixing studies showing restriction with only 25% competent capsid subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C178 synthesize prior imaging studies with the current study's structural data to estimate binding requirements. The estimates are reasonable and appropriately qualified, with good support from cited CA mixing studies.

results.result: TRIM5 restriction proceeds via a multi-step pathway where capsid recognition is followed by ubiquitin-dependent signaling leading to capsid dissociation and reverse transcription inhibition. Capsid binding can activate TRIM5 E3 ligase activity, and the hexagonal lattice structure suggests how this occurs through RING domain associations at three-fold vertices, supported by evidence for autoubiquitylation and B-box 2 trimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C192 synthesize prior mechanistic studies with the current structural findings to propose how lattice formation activates ubiquitin signaling. While some mechanistic details remain speculative (C190, C193), the overall model is well-supported by the combination of structural data and cited functional studies.
